name: Space Colonization

lumenary.blurb: A scatter of seeds of food, and a branch that grows toward whichever ones are closest. When a branch reaches a seed, the seed is eaten. Trees and leaf veins grow this way.

facts.bestOn: Dark shapes on a light ground

why: Plants compete for light, and a branch grows toward open space. The algorithm scatters food and lets branches grow toward the nearest food they can sense. When a branch reaches a morsel it eats it, so the next branch has to reach further. This is enough to make trees, roots and the veins of a leaf, and the picture decides where the food is.
how: Scatter attractors (food), thicker where you want growth, and start a few nodes at the roots.
Each round, every attractor finds the nearest node within the sensing distance.
Every node with at least one attractor in its care grows a new node a step D away, in the direction of the sum of the unit vectors toward its attractors.
Remove any attractor that comes within 2.4 D of a node.
Stop when no attractor is influencing anything, after 900 rounds, or at 40,000 nodes, and thicken the branches near the root.
history: Adam Runions and colleagues described the venation algorithm for leaves in 2005, and Runions, Brendan Lane and Przemyslaw Prusinkiewicz extended it to trees in 2007. It has been used for procedural plants in films and games, and for modelling blood vessels, rivers, roads and lightning.
uses: Procedural trees, roots and leaf veins
Modelling rivers, blood vessels and road networks
terms: A point of food that branches grow toward.
The pattern of veins in a leaf.
Generated by rules, not drawn by hand.
paragraphs: In 2007 Adam Runions and colleagues described how veins in a leaf and branches in a tree can be grown by competition for space. Scatter a cloud of attractors (the food), thick where you want growth. Start a few nodes at the roots. Each round, every attractor finds the nearest node within a sensing distance (the reach slider, a share of the picture’s width), and every node with at least one attractor in its care grows a new node: a step D away in the direction of the sum of the unit vectors to its attractors, with a tiny jitter. Any attractor that comes within 2.4 D of a node is eaten. The loop ends when no attractor is influencing anything, after 900 rounds, or at 40,000 nodes.

The picture decides where the food is: an attractor is kept with probability (1 − f) + f (0.03 + 0.97 h^1.4), where h is the heaviness of the picture there, so branches grow toward the dark parts and the picture appears as the density of the network. The roots can be along the bottom, in the middle (a vein network) or all around the edge. For thickness the program counts the descendants of each node, and draws a branch with a width proportional to the square root of that count: the cross-section area then adds up at every junction, which is Leonardo da Vinci’s rule for tree branches. Each segment takes the picture’s colour.

equations.tex: \mathbf n_v=\sum_{a\in S(v)}\frac{\mathbf a-\mathbf v}{\lVert\mathbf a-\mathbf v\rVert},\qquad \mathbf v_{\text{new}}=\mathbf v+D\,\frac{\mathbf n_v}{\lVert\mathbf n_v\rVert}
equations.note: Growth of node v toward the attractors S(v) that it is nearest to (within the sensing distance).
Branch width from the number c of nodes it feeds, so that areas add up at junctions.

dials.label: How far a branch can sense

presets.text: Roots at the bottom grow a tree upward.
Roots on the edges grow inward like frost.
A short reach makes dense, fine veins.
